analysis.one_liner: Strengthens legal remedies for workplace sexual harassment and funds rape prevention, domestic violence shelters, and safer campuses.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan women's rights package with 21 cosponsors (17 Republicans, 4 Democrats) sat in four House committees for nearly two years, was sent to five subcommittees, and never got a hearing or a vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let victims of workplace sexual harassment sue for money damages of up to $100,000 for a first offense and $150,000 for repeat offenses, and get a fast court order stopping the harassment without first waiting out the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission process [S2] [S3]. It would have made colleges report sexual assaults to students and parents, expanded federal penalties for sex offenses, made shelters and rape-prevention programs better funded, and created a Glass Ceiling Commission to study why women and minorities rarely reach executive jobs [S2] [S3]. It also would have applied sexual-harassment law to Congress itself, which was then exempt [S2] [S3]. The bill was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced, spent 16 months being passed between five subcommittees, and died without ever coming up for a vote [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed: women enduring sexual harassment at work (new money damages and fast court orders), victims of domestic violence (shelters in rural areas guaranteed 20% of funds, cross-state enforcement of protective orders, public-awareness campaigns), sexual assault victims (free HIV tests and counseling, state-paid forensic exams, $25 million a year in rape-prevention grants), students and parents (mandatory campus sexual-assault statistics), congressional employees (Title VII coverage), and women and minorities seeking entry into union apprenticeship programs (outreach grants) [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Creates money penalties for intentional sexual harassment — up to $100,000 for a first offense by an employer and $150,000 for each repeat offense — where before, victims often could only get an order telling the employer to stop.
Lets a harassment victim ask a court for an immediate order to stop the harassment without waiting for the EEOC to issue a right-to-sue letter, and requires courts to expedite these cases.
Applies Title VII employment discrimination law to Congress itself, ending the exemption of congressional offices from sexual-harassment law.
Requires colleges receiving federal aid to collect and publish statistics on rape and sexual assault and give the reports to students, parents or guardians, and local police.

Authorizes $25 million a year in grants for rape prevention and education, with at least 15% aimed at junior high and high school students, and requires states to pay the full cost of forensic exams for sexual assault victims.
Requires every state court to give full faith and credit to domestic violence protective orders issued in other states, so an order protects a victim who moves.
Guarantees at least 20% of family violence shelter funds go to rural areas and guarantees at least $1 million a year for Indian tribes, and funds public-information campaigns on domestic violence.

Establishes a Glass Ceiling Commission to study barriers to advancing women and minorities into executive management, and a Labor Department program with grants to recruit women and minorities into registered apprenticeships.
Expands federal civil rights law so discrimination in carrying out or changing a contract violates federal law, and extends the time limit for challenging discriminatory seniority systems.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed: employers found to have intentionally engaged in sexual harassment would pay up to $150,000 per offense in penalties and face faster court orders; producers, distributors, and sellers of sexually explicit material would face new civil lawsuits from victims of sex crimes, with damages, attorney's fees, and a lower burden of proof; the federal treasury would fund the grants, task force, and commission; and states would cover forensic exams for rape victims [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers and the adult media industry

drawbacks.text: The Pornography Victims' Compensation Act subtitle would let victims sue producers, distributors, exhibitors, and sellers of sexually explicit material for downstream sex crimes on a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard, with liability inferred from 'extraordinary similarities' between the material and the crime or expert testimony — a low bar that could impose ruinous liability on distant sellers who never touched the offender, and that courts were likely to strike down as inconsistent with First Amendment doctrine protecting even offensive non-obscene speech.

The bill expands the federal death penalty to murders committed in the course of sexual assaults or child molestations, with sentences guided by racial and gender-blindness certifications from jurors; death penalty expansion carries the risk of irreversible error and, at the time, would have applied to federal-jurisdiction cases only, reaching few actual cases.

New Federal Rules of Evidence would make a defendant's prior sexual assault or child molestation offenses admissible 'for its bearing on any matter' in later sex-crime cases — later enacted separately in 1994 and criticized since for inviting jury decisions based on character rather than proof of the charged act.

The harassment damages would only flow after the victim first used any employer grievance procedure or showed it was inadequate, a step that could delay recovery, and awards are capped and left to judicial discretion.
Its child-custody provision is only a non-binding 'sense of the Congress' that abuse evidence should create a presumption against custody for the abuser — symbolic language States could ignore.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The harassment remedies, campus reporting, protective-order enforcement, and prevention funding are concrete, practical protections whose costs fall mostly on employers who actually harass and on modest federal appropriations. The weakest parts are the pornography liability provision, which inverts the usual burden of proof for speech-based cases and would likely have failed in court while chilling lawful sellers, and the death penalty expansion, which is more punitive symbolism than measurable protection. On balance the bill's core would have meaningfully helped women workers and crime victims, but it was a grab-bag that bundled strong civil-rights provisions with constitutionally doubtful ones.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to four House committees the day it was introduced, bounced among five subcommittees over 16 months, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Susan Molinari, a New York Republican, introduced the Women's Equal Opportunity Act of 1991 on February 27, 1991, with 21 cosponsors — 17 Republicans and 4 Democrats.
That same day the bill was referred jointly to four House committees: Judiciary, Education and Labor, House Administration, and Energy and Commerce.

Over the following 16 months it was referred to five different subcommittees — Health and the Environment, Personnel and Police, Postsecondary Education, Select Education, and Employment Opportunities — and finally, on July 8, 1992, the Judiciary Subcommittee on Civil and Constitutional Rights.
No hearing, markup, or vote of any kind is recorded; the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who sexually harass employees keep working under a legal regime where victims generally could not recover money damages, and producers and sellers of sexually explicit material face no civil liability to victims of sex crimes. Congressional offices also remained exempt from Title VII sexual-harassment suits.

for.name: Rep. Susan Molinari
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Women's Equal Opportunity Act of 1991, combining sexual-harassment remedies, anti-violence programs, and workplace opportunity measures in one bill.

against.name: Rep. Jack Brooks
against.what_they_did: The Judiciary Committee received the bill on the day of introduction; the record shows it was sent to a subcommittee and, 16 months later, to another subcommittee, with no markup or hearing ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. William D. Ford
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: The Education and Labor Committee received the bill and referred it to three subcommittees (Postsecondary Education, Select Education, Employment Opportunities); no committee action beyond that is recorded.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of any final decision is unknown; sponsorship leaned Republican (17 Republicans and 4 Democrats signed on), and the bill died in committees controlled by the Democratic majority.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed monetary penalties of up to $100,000/$150,000 per offense for intentional sexual harassment and let victims get fast court orders without an EEOC right-to-sue letter. Harassment is not an ordinary cost of doing business — its victims are the employer's own workers — so this industry interest ran directly against the people the bill protects. Small employers (under 50 workers) would have gotten EEOC technical assistance to comply.

industries.industry: Producers, distributors, and sellers of sexually explicit material
industries.note: The Pornography Victims' Compensation Act subtitle would have created a federal civil cause of action letting victims of sex crimes sue anyone in the distribution chain for damages and attorney's fees. The industry's interest in killing or diluting this subtitle ran directly against victims seeking compensation.

Institutions receiving federal aid would have to collect and publish campus rape and sexual assault statistics and report them to students, parents, and police. That is a modest compliance burden that buys transparency students and families currently lack.

industries.industry: Registered apprenticeship sponsors (building trades and industry programs)
industries.note: The bill authorizes federal grants to pay for outreach, recruitment, and preapprenticeship training aimed at bringing women and minorities into registered programs. Sponsors get funded pipelines; the public gets wider access to skilled-trade careers.

industries.industry: Rape crisis centers and domestic violence shelters
industries.note: New $25 million-a-year rape prevention grants and expanded domestic violence demonstration grants would flow to these nonprofit providers, with guaranteed rural funding shares and a $1 million floor for Indian tribes. Victims get services; providers get revenue.
